title: Growing Scholarly Critique of Murray Thesis: Turning Point in Witchcraft Historiography
description:
By the late 1940s and through the 1950s, professional scholars were increasingly challenging Margaret Murray's witch-cult thesis through detailed archival and textual critique, marking a turning point in the historiography of witchcraft from popular mythology toward rigorous historical analysis. Russell Hope Robbins, an American scholar, began the systematic archival research that would culminate in his Encyclopedia of Witchcraft and Demonology (1959), which drew on extensive documentary evidence to provide a detailed account of actual witch trials that bore no resemblance to Murray's fertility-cult thesis. Robbins was highly critical of Murray and helped create space for empirically grounded scholarship.

The critique of Murray was not merely about her specific claims but about the methodological approach she represented: treating confessions extracted under torture as reliable ethnographic sources, selecting only evidence that supported a predetermined conclusion, and constructing a grand unified theory from fragmentary and contradictory evidence. The scholars who challenged her modeled a different approach — close reading of local records, attention to the legal and social context of trial documents, and skepticism about testimony produced under coercive conditions. This methodological shift set the stage for the social-historical revolution in witchcraft studies that would come with Thomas and Macfarlane in 1971.

The period also saw the development of a Continental scholarly tradition of witchcraft research that would eventually intersect with the English-language scholarship. Joseph Hansen's earlier archival work had already established rigorous documentary foundations, and scholars like Will-Erich Peuckert and later German and Dutch historians were developing empirically grounded accounts of specific trials and regions that Murray's sweeping synthesis made impossible.
historiographical_note: The transition from the Murray-influenced popular tradition to rigorous historical scholarship has been mapped by Ronald Hutton in The Triumph of the Moon and by Brian Levack in his surveys of the field. The period 1948-1960 represents a crucial but often under-recognized phase when archival and documentary scholarship was accumulating the evidence base that would support the social-historical revolution of the early 1970s. Norman Cohn's eventual synthesis in Europe's Inner Demons (1975) built on this accumulation of critique.
source_method: Published scholarship including Robbins (1959); historiographical surveys by Hutton and Levack
